lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1943, America's most secret missile guidance system was three pigeons.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It started on a train in 1940. A psychologist called B. F. Skinner watched a flock of birds flying alongside him.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Birds have amazing eyesight, he thought. Could one of them steer a bomb?

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So he trained pigeons to peck at a picture of a target. Every good peck earned a few grains of food.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then he built a missile around them. A lens in the nose showed the bird the view ahead, and its pecks steered the missile.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In case one pigeon got distracted, there were three of them. They voted.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: So the missile was run by a committee. Of pigeons.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The flour company General Mills gave him the top floor of a mill in Minneapolis to train them. Then the government put in twenty-five thousand dollars.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: At the big demonstration in Washington, the pigeon tracked its target perfectly. The scientists watching still couldn't take it seriously.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then, in 1948, the Navy brought the pigeons back, and kept them until 1953, when electronic guidance finally won.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Skinner kept some of his birds. Years later, he tested them again. They still went straight for the target.
